title: Rocky Marciano, multiculturalism and Coming to America (1988).

commenti.body: Sometimes just because an athlete does not see themselves as a “great white hope” doesn’t mean they aren’t if that makes sense. Like Larry bird is by all means not a racist at all. If you ever watch that bird Vs Magic doc. It’s clear that man has no racism in his heart. However their were plenty of Celtics fans who did and loved bird which made the black community view bird in a negative light. Which is what I imagine happened to Marciano by the 80s.
I think that is a good point. The interesting thing with Marciano was his ability to defeat men who were far better boxers than him with his relentless remorseless punching power and endurance.

>Celtics fans

That's still a major issue in Boston. It's like the last stronghold in the NBA for that kind of culture.

That’s an interesting take.  I’m sure you know, but I’ll just point out that Marciano’s reign as champion was over 30 years before the movie came out.  Those small gestures of respect that he made were only remembered by boxing diehards.  For most people, the era of a white heavyweight champion was long ago.  Ali and Tyson were the ones who most moviegoers would recognize by the time that Coming To America came out

It’s the fact that Marciano is the only undisputed heavyweight boxing champion to retire undefeated.

That combined with his KO record enshrines his immortality.

When the ever confident Ali admits he isn’t sure if he can beat you, that says something.

Admittedly my boxing history is really hazy before the 60’s but didn’t Rocky Marciano mainly fight scrubs and bums? At least that’s what the old boys at my local pub tell me.

I mean it really says something when his most famous fight was against a washed out Joe Louis (*who according to the barber in Coming to America was 137 years old*).

The 50’s in general is seen as a mediocre decade for heavyweights they were nothing compared to the 60’s/70’s titans hence why Sugar Ray Robinson a middleweight is the most famous of that era.

Boxing is quite a difficult sport to measure because your only really as good as the opponents you fight hence why Ali’s legacy is so cemented because he fought titans like Frazier, Liston, Holmes. Marciano just doesn’t have that track record.

Believe me it’s alive and well in boxing as well, I’ll never forget the Mayweather vs Mcregor fight, so much dog whistling online it was astounding. if that fight occurred 100 years ago it would have caused riots like Johnson vs Jeffries.

> Which is what I imagine happened to Marciano by the 80s.

I have attended the Marciano tournament in my area the past few years and getting into boxing in general. The head coaches are both white guys but they'll be the first to admit a lot of people in boxing from the officials to the fans are dumb and racist. Same thing with Bird as you point out, Boston and New England in general have a lot of racists who like sports, racist being a term with more breadth than depth here.

Marciano’s resume was decent I’d say.  His best wins were against aging guys, but they generally weren’t shot fighters and still formidable. 

Joe Louis was on the comeback trail, and had some okay wins, but was a shell of his prior self.  Actually, he was never really the same after WW2.  If he stayed active during WW2 and kept winning, he could have ended up with 30-35 title defenses.

Jersey Joe Walcott was 37, but peaked relatively old.  I don’t think he had time to fully focus on his boxing career when he was younger. 
Ezzard Charles was arguably the greatest LHW ever, and a very good heavyweight champ.  He was aging though.  Archie Moore is not too far behind Ezzard on the all-time LHW list, and had a nice run at HW to become a legit contender.  He was either 38 or 41 (depending if you go by the 1913 or 1916 birthdate).  The gap in weight between LHW and HW wasn’t as large back then.  

Despite being the glamour division of boxing, I don’t really hear HWs being talked about as having so many strong eras like other divisions.  You hear about the early to mid 70s, and early to mid 90s, but usually people talk about eras being weak or average in talent.  

While I’d say Marciano‘s small size and style would hurt him against a lot of great HWs in history, I think he would have been a monster at cruiserweight
If their isn't many good players from an ethic background, it's reasonable for people up that ethnic background to feel pride at someone who is like them succeeding

rocky marciano's respect for his black opponents and his refusal to embrace the great white hope idea is truly commendable. it's interesting to see how he valued representing everyone, regardless of race.

How much of an option was it for him to be a great white hope in real time? Was it talked about?

Marciano was Italian-American fighting in the early 1950s. Probably considered "white" by then, but probably still othered by and large by America.

My understanding is that a generation of boxers were killed in WWII, so Marciano did fight some over the hill fighters in the 1950s - not because he was avoiding anyone but because they were the best around until a new generation of great heavyweights came along in the 1960s

rocky marciano definitely doesn't get enough credit for his respect towards his black opponents. it's refreshing to see a white champion who truly treated everyone as equals. his actions spoke louder than any words.
